rows.proposal:
Your main challenge is making Transformer inference practical to operate—not just wrapping a model in an endpoint. I can start with a consultation to understand your current APIs, model workloads, and deployment constraints, then agree on an implementation scope and timeline before the build expands.

Relevant work includes model-shelf, a FastAPI service that queues Transformer jobs with Celery and Redis, manages model residency within a GPU memory budget, and exposes Prometheus metrics [repo-04]. In a related multi-model inference project, the case study reports 410 ms p95 extraction latency under 40 concurrent requests and a 41% infrastructure cost reduction [cs-10]. I’ve also built a PostgreSQL/pgvector-backed question-answering project [repo-01].

For implementation, I’d review the existing routes and workloads, then propose a phased plan covering API structure and validation, performance testing, monitoring, security, and deployment. We can confirm the specific requirements, timeline, and budget after the consultation.

I can build a scoped MVP covering face detection and visibility checks, replay/print liveness checks, documented REST endpoints, PM2 process management, reason codes, and an evaluation report. I’ve delivered a face-onboarding service that checked visibility and combined a random blink/head-turn challenge with a texture classifier for screen and print spoofing [cs-06]. On that project’s hold-out set, it rejected 96% of replay attacks and 98% of print attacks, with a 1.8% genuine-user false rejection rate; processing was about 180 ms per frame on CPU [cs-06]. These are results from that project, not guarantees for this one.

For the $1,000 fixed budget, I’d first agree on the target hardware, input format, dataset, and acceptance criteria. Then I’d implement and test the MVP, document thresholds and error handling, and provide guidance for collecting and labeling additional data. FPS and accuracy targets should be validated on your target hardware and data; uncertain cases can return a review-needed result rather than an automatic pass or rejection.

You need a continuously available service that keeps the right Hugging Face models loaded at the right times, while managing GPU memory and giving operators a clear view of what is running. I’ve built a queued, multi-model Hugging Face service with on-demand loading and unloading, scheduled residency, GPU memory limits, and an admin page showing resident models [cs-10]. A related FastAPI implementation uses timetable-based model pinning, Celery/Redis queues, and LRU eviction [repo-04]. In the case study, five models shared a 24 GB GPU; measured latency was 120 ms median for classification and 410 ms p95 for extraction under 40 concurrent requests [cs-10].

I’d start by confirming your model list, GPU limits, and required text/image input-output paths. Then I’d build model-specific adapters, scheduled loading, inference endpoints, and an operator UI. I’d benchmark representative workloads and tune batching and precision against your latency and memory targets. For image workflows, I’d scope the adapters around the Hugging Face models you select.

What GPU hardware and model list are you targeting?

Your live RTSP feed may be skipping because detection is processing buffered frames instead of the newest frame. I’ve addressed this same issue in a YOLOv8 counting deployment by moving capture into a background thread, keeping only the latest frame, adding reconnect handling, and enabling half-precision inference. Throughput increased from 14 to 25 FPS per stream across two docks on an RTX 3060 (cs-05). My dock-counter repo also demonstrates YOLOv8 tracking and line-crossing counts over RTSP with a latest-frame reader and reconnect behavior (repo-03).

I’d first inspect your stream reader, inference time, hardware utilization, resolution, and model settings. Then I’d adapt the pipeline and test it on your hardware and sample footage, focusing on reducing latency while preserving your existing detection and counting workflow. I’ll flag any requirements that would expand the scope.

My fixed bid is $150, the minimum for this engagement. Since the posted budget is $60, please confirm whether you can increase it before we start.

Not bidding. The role requires teaching experience and six months of onsite availability in Slavonia, neither of which is evidenced in the available profile. The client’s history also gives reason for caution.

If this project is still active, I can build a focused MVP: a web chat interface grounded in the linked Volvo comparison page, with a basic speech-to-text and text-to-speech flow. I’d confirm your web framework and preferred voice provider first, and keep the $150 scope to one source page and one app surface. My relevant work includes a product-support chat widget using indexed catalogue content [cs-03], a voice assistant integrating transcription and speech synthesis [cs-11], and a LangChain-based retrieval assistant [cs-13].

Your goal—filtering about 100 Telegram notifications a day down to the few worth seeing—is feasible with a Telegram-to-AI triage workflow.

I built a similar system that monitored four Telegram channels, classified messages with an LLM, and forwarded selected items with a summary and original link to a private channel. The client supplied labeled examples; on a held-out evaluation set, the actionable category reached 0.89 precision and 0.94 recall. [cs-15]

I’d start by confirming how the three source channels can be accessed and what you consider valuable, ideally using examples of messages you would and wouldn’t want forwarded. Then I’d implement ingestion, classification, forwarding to your destination channel, and a way to review borderline results. I estimate 12–18 hours for an initial working version, including testing; I can refine that after reviewing sample notifications and access requirements. My rate is $35/hour.
Do not bid: the role centers on accounting, payroll, and bilingual English-Spanish skills that are not supported by the freelancer’s profile.
I’m not proceeding with an unpaid, end-to-end trial that requires a deployed bot and repository before a contract. I’d consider a clearly scoped paid trial under contract instead.
No proposal. The post asks applicants to move communication and payment off-platform, including via Telegram and USDT or bank transfer. I would not contact them there or share personal information.

Your team needs reliable answers across Confluence and PDF documentation, with citations and a way to measure retrieval quality. I’d build a source-aware ingestion pipeline and FastAPI chat API backed by Postgres/pgvector, with grounded answers, citations, and a clear fallback when the documents don’t contain an answer. I’d also prepare the requested 50-question evaluation set and a concise handover covering setup, ingestion, configuration, and operation. At kickoff, I’d confirm Confluence API access, space scope, and permission requirements so ingestion is designed appropriately. My portfolio includes a PDF RAG implementation using pgvector with cited answers; FastAPI and evaluation design are also among my listed skills. I can work toward your three-week timeline, with scope and access confirmed at kickoff.

I’d start by reviewing the label format, class balance, image quality, and train/validation split, then fine-tune a YOLOv8 baseline and evaluate class-wise errors. Deliverables would include per-class precision and recall, a confusion matrix, validation examples, and a small FastAPI inference endpoint with setup and usage notes. I can target the 2–3 week timeline, assuming data access and usable labels are ready.

My relevant work includes training YOLOv8 on 2,300 hand-labelled camera frames [cs-05]. My CV lists PyTorch and FastAPI and describes shipped object-detection systems exposed over HTTP [cv]. I’ve also implemented a FastAPI inference service [repo-04]. These examples aren’t PCB-specific, so I’d validate performance on your held-out images rather than assume results transfer.

Fixed price: $1,200.

I can build the Zendesk-to-Slack workflow to summarize new tickets, classify urgency, and deliver twice-daily digests. I’d include rate-limit-aware retries and caching keyed to ticket content so unchanged tickets aren’t repeatedly sent to the LLM.

A relevant analogue: I built an LLM triage service that classified about 600 Telegram messages a day, summarized actionable items, and deduplicated messages—removing about 22% of forwards while keeping monthly model spend around $9. I’ve also built an LLM messaging bot with Redis-backed state, and my background includes Python and support-ticket text classification.

I’d confirm your urgency categories, expected ticket volume, Slack channel, and digest timezone first. Then I’d use the stated 25-hour scope for integration, implementation, and testing. My rate is $45/hour.

Your challenge is to turn 60,000 labeled reviews into a useful three-class classifier—and deliver something your team can run, not just a model score.

I’d fine-tune a transformer, evaluate it on a held-out set using macro F1 and per-class metrics, then package the model behind a REST endpoint. I’ve done closely related work: for a hotel group, I fine-tuned a multilingual transformer for review sentiment and achieved 0.89 macro F1 on polarity [cs-14]. In a separate BERT classification project, I reached 0.87 macro F1 and deployed the model behind an async HTTP endpoint [cs-04].

The handoff would include a reproducible notebook, saved model and tokenizer weights, and an API implementation with setup instructions. I’d keep the test set separate until final evaluation and report the measured results rather than promise a predetermined accuracy. I can complete this within two weeks for your $700 fixed budget, assuming the labeled data and class definitions are ready to use.
